transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-11 14:00 UTC | Duration: 48 mins | Attendees: Lara Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Rivera (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (QuantaHealth Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Platform Eng), Marta Ruiz (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Lara Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we were told QuantaHealth wanted a compact walkthrough of how we pick open models and how the compatibility heatmap helps you narrow candidates — I'm Lara AE, with Marcus SE.
[00:07] Nina Patel: Hi Lara, hi Marcus, thanks. We want to get through the catalog, then see how to interpret bench numbers for our summarization pipeline. Timebox 45-ish.
[00:12] Marcus Rivera: Great, I'll share my screen — pulling up Console > Models > Compatibility heatmap. Quick note, apologies if labels are fuzzy, the internal name mapping sometimes has minor mismatches in the view.
[00:22] Ethan Brooks: That's fine, just FYI we run on GKE with private subnets, and we have a 99th percentile latency SLO around 600ms for 512-token prompts.
[00:30] Marta Ruiz: And we need a KMS integration and audit logs for any PII processing. Also, SOC2 is a must for production.

[00:40] Marcus Rivera: Understood — we map those constraints to routing policies and dedicated profiles. Okay heatmap up: rows are models, columns are workload profiles — summarization/QA/embedding — colors indicate compatibility score (green = recommended, amber = borderline, red = poor). Note: the score is composite — latency estimate, token cost, eval score on a small calibration set.
[00:55] Nina Patel: That "composite" — can you unpack weights? Which factor dominates?
[01:03] Marcus Rivera: Sure, by default for Console Optimize the weights are latency 40%, quality 40%, cost 20%. You can adjust per-workspace — many customers bias quality up for clinical text. Also note kernel compatibility and quantization support influences the latency estimate — e.g., some 4-bit quantized variants can be faster but degrade certain safety tokens.
[01:22] Lara Chen: Also worth noting: the heatmap flags models that have partial feature mismatches, like missing function calling or output schema enforcement — those show as hatch marks.

[01:35] Nina Patel: We do need structured output (JSON summary + confidence) for downstream ingestion. How do you represent that capability?
[01:42] Marcus Rivera: There's a column for 'structured-output fidelity' — it's 0-100 based on evals with your prompt set, but for customers we recommend an explicit small eval because out-of-the-box numbers are noisy. We'll ask you to share a sample prompt set.
[01:55] Ethan Brooks: When you say 'evals are noisy' — is that tokenization mismatch? We use byte-level tokenization and sometimes Open-source forks have different tokenizers.
[02:04] Marcus Rivera: Exactly, tokenization and prompt length distribution affect both token cost and accuracy. That's why our bench script includes a tokenization step that normalizes to model's tokenizer. We'll provide a bench harness.

[02:18] Marta Ruiz: For private deployment, do we get the same heatmap? We can't send data to hosted service for the mapping.
[02:25] Lara Chen: Good question — for Private deployments we can run the same compatibility scanner inside your VPC, it requires a short agent that runs bench flows on your infra. We also offer sanitized synthetic data mode if you prefer.
[02:38] Nina Patel: What's the timeline to run a one-week pilot?
[02:43] Lara Chen: For a 1-week dedicated pilot, we typically provision a small Dedicated pool, run a 24-hour calibration bench, then deploy a canary for live traffic with routing rules. So prep + infra + bench is usually 3–5 business days.

[02:55] Marcus Rivera: Ok I'm pulling up an example heatmap we did for a finance customer — you'll notice the top row models are small Llama-derivatives — they look green for cost/latency but amber for summarization quality. The higher-quality models show as green for our clinical eval but cost more.
[03:15] Nina Patel: Is there a way to pin a model for production but have an automatic fallback to cheaper variant on heavy load?
[03:22] Marcus Rivera: Yes — routing policies support pinning plus fallbacks. There's also a 'graceful degrade' policy where for tail-latency spikes we route to a lower-cost variant that supports the same output schema. We preserve KV cache semantics when models are ABI-compatible, otherwise we rehydrate context which affects latency.
[03:40] Ethan Brooks: ABI-compatible — can you clarify?
[03:43] Marcus Rivera: ABI as in same tokenizer, same KV cache format. When you switch between models compiled to different kernels/quantization, cache can't be reused. We show compatibility in the heatmap and flag cache-retention score.
[03:55] Marta Ruiz: About encryption — will audit logs include per-token redaction markers? We need proof we didn't store PII.
[04:02] Lara Chen: Audit logs include request/response hashes and metadata, but not full plaintext unless you enable that. For PII we recommend client-side redaction before sending or sending to Private where logs can be controlled. We integrate with customer KMS for key rotation.

[04:20] Nina Patel: Can we see an example bench output? Small sample please.
[04:25] Marcus Rivera: I'll paste a snippet — "model: open-llama-30b-4bit, mean-latency: 220ms@256, p99: 610ms@512, quality: 0.81 (ROUGE-L-like), token-cost: $0.003/token-equivalent"
[04:46] Ethan Brooks: So that one p99 610ms is too high — could quantization or kernel choice improve p99?
[04:52] Marcus Rivera: Sometimes switching to a kernel that has better attention streaming reduces tail. Also batching parameters and prefilling KV cache for repeated context helps. For dedicated infra we can tune kernel selection per model variant to shave p99 by ~10-25% in many cases.
[05:08] Nina Patel: If we pick a higher-quality model but it costs 3x, can Optimize suggest a quantized variant that keeps quality within a delta?
[05:15] Marcus Rivera: Yes, Optimize suggests quantization profiles with estimated quality deltas — we show a tradeoff curve. For clinical summarization many customers accept a 1-2% quality drop for ~40-60% lower token cost.
[05:27] Lara Chen: I'm toggling the sidebar to show 'recommendations' — here Optimize suggests 'open-med-13b-quant-qlora' for your summarization sample, with fallback to 'open-med-7b-quant' during bursts.
[05:38] Nina Patel: "open-med" — are those models curated by Redwood or community-uploaded? We have legal constraints about model provenance.
[05:45] Lara Chen: We maintain a model catalog — some are community open models, some Redwood-curated variants with verification. For enterprise we provide provenance metadata (training license, weights URL, vetting notes). That's included in the model detail pane.
[05:59] Marta Ruiz: About licenses — do you provide a summary of license risk? Some Open weights are Apache, some are unclear.
[06:06] Marcus Rivera: We annotate license type; for ambiguous ones we flag them 'review required' and include notes. We can export a compliance report per selected model list.
[06:16] Nina Patel: If we run bench in our VPC, will Redwood see results?
[06:20] Lara Chen: No, for Private mode bench results stay in your control. For Hosted/Dedicated we can optionally collect anonymized telemetry if you opt in.
[06:29] Ethan Brooks: On the integration side: how do we route requests from our service to Redwood Dedicated? Do you provide SDK and proxy?
[06:34] Marcus Rivera: We have SDKs (Python/Go/JS) and a lightweight sidecar that can run in your cluster to manage routing and secrets. For VPC peering we have a private endpoint, and a sidecar handles auth and KMS.
[06:47] Nina Patel: Let's talk about benchmarks: what's in the bench harness? Are you running multi-turn?
[06:52] Marcus Rivera: Bench harness is configurable: single-turn, multi-turn, structured output checks, hallucination tests, and stress tests for concurrency. We also simulate tokenization differences and measure token cost.
[07:05] Lara Chen: Quick demo: I'm switching to the 'bench compare' view showing three candidates and a delta chart of quality vs cost. Notice the bubble sizes represent memory footprint.
[07:15] Nina Patel: I like the visualization. Can we export the data as CSV for our ML team to ingest?
[07:20] Marcus Rivera: Yes — 'export bench CSV' and an XLSX with per-sample breakdown. I'll add that to the action items.
[07:27] Marta Ruiz: For pilot, we need SOC2 and network diagrams before infra changes.
[07:31] Lara Chen: We'll send SOC2 docs and the Private deployment checklist (network diagram template) as part of the security packet.
[07:38] Ethan Brooks: On cost reporting — can Console provide token-level cost attribution by route/feature?
[07:43] Marcus Rivera: Yes — Console shows per-route cost breakdown and token-level charts, and you can query cost by model version and deployment mode.
[07:53] Nina Patel: Let's make this concrete — what's the minimal config to start a 1-week pilot?
[07:58] Lara Chen: Proposal: 1) Provision a 2-GPU Dedicated pool (NVIDIA H100 or equivalent) with autoscaling to 4 during bench; 2) Run 48h calibration bench with your prompt set and our harness; 3) Canary deploy one route with 5% traffic for 3 days then ramp. We'll provide a price estimate for that.
[08:18] Ethan Brooks: Do you support on-prem bare metal for H100? Our infra team might prefer that.
[08:22] Marcus Rivera: Yes — Private on-prem is supported but timeline is longer due to network and HSM setup. For short pilot Dedicated is fastest.
[08:30] Nina Patel: Okay sounds good. Could you also check that the recommended model supports JSON output with coarse confidence?
[08:36] Marcus Rivera: Will do — I'll run a targeted eval for structured-output fidelity and include examples.
[08:42] Lara Chen: Quick recap — we'll send the heatmap export + bench CSV, SOC2 and private deploy checklist, and Marcus will share bench harness and run a targeted eval once you provide sample prompts/data distribution. We'll schedule pilot kickoff next week if this looks good.
[08:58] Nina Patel: Thanks, this was helpful. One last question — competitor differences: Anthropic had good safety for hallucinations, any notes?
[09:05] Marcus Rivera: We annotate safety profiles and add safety evals; Redwood's runtime supports safety filters and function-based grounding to mitigate hallucinations in post-processing. We'll include a safety eval pass in the bench.
[09:17] Marta Ruiz: Please include a data retention policy doc.
[09:20] Lara Chen: Will do.
[09:23] Nina Patel: Great, look forward to the files. Thanks Lara, Marcus.
[09:26] Lara Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts.

[END]
